Problem 5 Water-Molecule Cages (24 points, 10%)
The cubic unit-cell structure of the alloy $Zr_3Au$ is shown below. Au atoms occupy the corners and body center of the cell. Each face contains 2 Zr atoms arranged symmetrically along a direction parallel to a coordinate axis (their three coordinates are 0, 1/2, and either 1/4 or 3/4).

header_images.description: Schematic cubic unit cell of the alloy $Zr_3Au$, drawn as a thin gray wireframe cube. Two kinds of glossy spheres are shown: dark, nearly black spheres near the cube corners and body center, and light gray-white spheres arranged symmetrically near the faces. Thin gray lines connect the spheres. The spheres carry no labels. At lower left is a three-colored coordinate triad: a red arrow points down-left and is labeled with a lowercase a, a green arrow points horizontally right and is labeled b, and a blue arrow points vertically upward and is labeled c. No other text appears in the image.

subquestions.text_open: 5.1 State the lattice type of crystalline $Zr_3Au$.
5.2 State the number of nearest, equidistant Zr atoms around each Au atom.
5.3 For each Zr atom, state separately the number of nearest, equidistant Au atoms, the number of nearest, equidistant Zr atoms, and the number of next-nearest, equidistant Zr atoms.

5.5 Replace every atomic position in $Zr_3Au$ with a methane molecule and place one water molecule at the center of each small tetrahedron described above. The resulting structure is that of methane hydrate. Write the formula of methane hydrate in the form $xCH_4\cdot yH_2O$.

5.6 The unit-cell parameter of methane hydrate is $a = 1.20\ \mathrm{nm}$. Calculate the maximum theoretical volume of methane gas that can be released from $1\ \mathrm{m^3}$ of methane hydrate at 273 K and 1 atm.

5.7 The cubic crystal of another similar hydrate can be described as follows. Hexadecahedra $[5^{12}6^4]$ whose vertices are water molecules (the notation denotes 12 pentagonal faces and 4 hexagonal faces; the polyhedron has the same symmetry as a regular tetrahedron and is shown below) are joined pairwise by sharing hexagonal faces, forming an infinite diamond-like structure. These hexadecahedra clearly do not fill all space: the four tetrahedral-void positions that are unoccupied in diamond remain. In fact, exactly four pentagonal dodecahedra, also with water molecules at their vertices, fit into each such void. The dodecahedra share pentagonal faces with one another and with the hexadecahedra, and each water molecule in the final structure is shared by four polyhedra. Place one $CCl_4$ molecule at the center of every hexadecahedron and one Xe atom at the center of every dodecahedron.
Structure of the hexadecahedron $[5^{12}6^4]$
5.7.1 Write the formula of this crystal in the form $xCCl_4\cdot yXe\cdot zH_2O$.

text_images.description: Wireframe representation of the hexadecahedron $[5^{12}6^4]$. Its vertices are shown as small hollow white circles with thin black outlines, and its edges as thin black lines. Edges facing the viewer are solid, while hidden rear edges are dashed. Alternating hexagonal and pentagonal faces form an approximately spherical cage. The image contains no text, numbers, arrows, or coordinate-axis labels.
